title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Net profit is an accounting opinion; free cash flow after working capital is the only verdict that pays dividends.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.text: Ten-Year Profit & Loss Forensics: Operating Profit vs. Other Income

web_blocks.html: From FY15 through FY26 and TTM September 2026, EIL's income statement shows cyclical operating margins cushioned by steady treasury returns [1]. Consolidated sales doubled from ₹1,741 crore in FY15 to ₹3,237 crore in FY20 [1]. Sales then stalled between ₹2,913 crore and ₹3,330 crore during FY21–FY25 before breaking out to ₹3,928 crore in FY26 [1]. A careful reader must check the line below operating profit: Other Income [1]. In FY26, Other Income of ₹242 crore made up 27.1% of consolidated Profit Before Tax (₹894 crore) [1]. On a TTM basis through September 2026, Other Income rose to ₹370 crore, or 32.7% of ₹1,130 crore PBT [1]. Interest on surplus cash and dividends from NRL and CIL are recurring, yet they are non-operating returns. They flatter pre-tax margins and return ratios relative to pure engineering profit [1, 15].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Profit & Loss Statement (FY15–FY26 & TTM)
web_blocks.takeaway: Consolidated sales grew 27% in FY26 to ₹3,928 Cr after five flat years, and OPM doubled from 9% in FY24 to 18% in FY26 (21% TTM). Still, Other Income supplies 27%–33% of PBT.

web_blocks.text: Balance Sheet Solvency, Strategic Investments & Contingent Claims

web_blocks.html: EIL's balance sheet holds deep liquidity and almost zero financial debt [1, 17]. Total borrowings stood at just ₹17 crore in March 2026 and ₹16 crore in September 2026 [1]. That compares with ₹3,341 crore of equity and reserves (₹281 crore equity capital plus ₹3,060 crore reserves) [1]. Total investments grew from ₹138 crore in FY15 to ₹1,606 crore in March 2026 and ₹1,707 crore in September 2026 [1, 18]. Those investments include EIL's equity stakes in RFCL (₹491 crore) and NRL (₹838.41 crore) plus treasury holdings [1, 18]. Fixed assets remain tiny at ₹334 crore in September 2026, proving the asset-light model [1]. One footnote item needs watching: Note 4 of the Q2 FY27 NSE filing lists a ₹40,960.75 lakh (₹409.61 crore) contractor claim before the Supreme Court [13]. Management states that contractor dues are reimbursable by the client under contract terms and expects no cash outflow [13].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Balance Sheet (FY15–Sep 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: EIL runs nearly debt-free (₹16 Cr debt vs. ₹3,341 Cr net worth and ₹1,707 Cr investments as of Sep 2026). Investors must still watch the ₹409.61 Cr Supreme Court claim.

web_blocks.text: Cash Flow Conversion & Working Capital Forensics

web_blocks.html: EIL's cash flow statement shows that working capital—not capex—drives annual cash conversion [1]. From FY15 to FY26, EIL produced ₹2,193 crore in total operating cash flow (CFO) and ₹1,950 crore in free cash flow (FCF) [1]. Yet annual CFO has swung sharply [1]. CFO fell to ₹48 crore in FY22 and turned negative at -₹113 crore in FY23 (only 7% of EBITDA) [1]. It recovered to ₹222 crore in FY24, dipped to ₹117 crore in FY25 (48% of EBITDA), and rebounded to ₹319 crore in FY26 (70% of EBITDA; ₹252 crore FCF) [1]. Client advances explain this swing [1]. EIL held deeply negative working capital days (-186 to -215 days in FY18–FY21) funded by upfront advances [1]. Those narrowed to -60 days by FY26 as advances normalized and debtor days rose from 37 days in FY24 to 45–53 days in FY25–FY26 [1].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Cash Flow Statement (FY15–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: Total FCF of ₹1,950 Cr over FY15–FY26 funds 40%–49% dividend payouts. However, annual CFO swings widely (7% to 205% of EBITDA) with client advances and contract assets.

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Return Ratios (FY15–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: ROCE reached 30% in FY26 (up from 22% in FY24) on higher consultancy margins. Negative working capital days narrowed from -186 days in FY21 to -60 days in FY26 as advances normalized.

web_blocks.mechanism: Aggressive bidding on fixed-price lump-sum turnkey (LSTK) EPC jobs met cost overruns and delayed client payments. Rising debt then wiped out equity buffers when operating margins turned negative.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: In H1 2024, Petrofac posted US$1,240M sales with a US$162M business-performance net loss (US$208M reported loss, -18.5% EBITDA margin). Net debt hit US$622M against US$164M cash, forcing EBITDA covenant waivers before restructuring [23].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Petrofac proves the lethal risk of fixed-price EPC paired with debt. EIL avoids that trap with zero net debt and by capping Turnkey at ~25%–32% of backlog, though underpriced LSTK bidding would erode cash [1, 15].

web_blocks.html: For an owner, EIL's clean balance sheet and 30.4% ROCE offer strong downside protection. Still, its 70% FY26 CFO/EBITDA conversion and ₹370 crore TTM Other Income require separating core engineering cash from treasury yield. That distinction shapes how the market prices this business.

Balance-sheet liquidity remains EIL's quietest strength. As of September 2026, consolidated investments stood at ₹1,707 Cr against just ₹16 Cr of borrowings [1][13]. That net-cash cushion earns steady treasury yields and funds bank guarantees for mega-projects without interest expense [1][17]. However, Note 4 of the Q2 FY27 results flags a ₹409.61 Cr claim before the Supreme Court [13]. An adverse ruling would absorb roughly 59% of FY26 PAT, making legal monitoring essential [1][13].

book_paragraphs: Now you and I are going to put on our forensic accountant hats and stress-test Engineers India Limited's ten-year financial record. When a company reports a 30.4% return on capital employed, a 23.4% return on equity, and virtually zero debt, it is tempting to stop digging. Resist that temptation. Good forensics means asking where the profits came from, whether they turned into cash, and what risks sit in the footnotes.

Start with the Profit and Loss statement. Between FY21 and FY25, EIL's sales barely moved, hovering around ₹2,913 crore to ₹3,330 crore, before breaking out 27% to ₹3,928 crore in FY26. Look one line below operating profit, however, and you will spot a crucial detail: Other Income. In FY26, EIL earned ₹242 crore in Other Income—27.1% of its entire ₹894 crore pre-tax profit. On a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026, Other Income hit ₹370 crore, or 32.7% of ₹1,130 crore pre-tax profit. That cash comes from interest on EIL's treasury pile and dividends from Numaligarh Refinery and Coal India. It is real money, and it cushions downturns, but you should never confuse treasury yield with engineering growth.

book_subsections.title: The Working Capital and Cash Conversion Puzzle
paragraphs: Next, look at the cash flow statement and working capital ratios together. Over twelve years from FY15 to FY26, EIL generated ₹2,193 crore in cumulative operating cash flow and ₹1,950 crore in cumulative free cash flow because its capital expenditure is tiny. That free cash flow comfortably funded dividend payouts of 38% to 49% in most normal years. Yet that cash did not arrive smoothly. In FY23, operating cash flow actually turned negative at minus ₹113 crore, converting just 7% of operating profit into cash. In FY25, it was ₹117 crore (48% conversion), before rebounding to ₹319 crore (70% conversion and ₹252 crore free cash flow) in FY26.

Why does cash conversion bounce around so much? The answer sits in Working Capital Days. Back in FY18 through FY21, EIL operated with negative working capital of minus 186 to minus 215 days—meaning clients gave EIL huge upfront cash advances before work was billed. By FY26, those negative working capital days compressed to minus 60 days as advances normalized and debtor days ticked up from 37 days in FY24 to 45–53 days in FY25–FY26. When client advances shrink, cash flow lags accounting profit; when new mega-orders bring fresh mobilization advances, cash flow surges.

book_subsections.title: A Balance Sheet Built to Survive What Sinks Peers
paragraphs: Finally, let us test EIL's balance sheet against the base rate of failure in global energy engineering. Look at Petrofac Limited, once a premier UK-listed oilfield EPC contractor. When fixed-price turnkey contracts ran into cost overruns and delayed collections, Petrofac's losses mounted—posting a US$162 million business-performance net loss (US$208 million reported loss) in the first half of 2024 on US$1,240 million of revenue—while US$622 million in net debt forced EBITDA covenant waivers and balance-sheet restructuring.

EIL is built to avoid that trap. With just ₹16 crore of borrowings against ₹3,341 crore of net worth and ₹1,707 crore of investments in September 2026 (including its ₹491 crore stake in RFCL and ₹838.41 crore stake in Numaligarh Refinery), EIL has no debt-service fragility. Keep an eye on one footnote item—Note 4 of the Q2 FY27 filing discloses a ₹409.61 crore contractor arbitration claim pending before the Supreme Court, which management expects to be reimbursable by the client—but recognize that EIL's net-cash discipline is its ultimate shock absorber.

book_subsections.title: Separating Core Engineering Cash from Treasury Income
paragraphs: A disciplined forensic reader never takes consolidated Profit Before Tax at face value when a company sits on more than ₹1,700 crore of balance-sheet investments. At EIL, interest and investment income routinely contribute 27 to 33 percent of pre-tax profit. That cash cushion is a genuine strength—it funds dividends, eliminates bankruptcy risk, and lets EIL bid on mega-projects without bank debt—but treasury yields are not an engineering moat.

When we strip out Other Income and look strictly at core operating profit, EIL's true earnings power has still improved markedly: operating profit rose from ₹299 crore in FY24 to ₹514 crore in FY25, ₹699 crore in FY26, and ₹803 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis. Pairing that rising core operating engine with a clean balance sheet—just ₹16 crore of borrowings—gives EIL genuine financial resilience, provided the ₹409.61 crore Supreme Court arbitration contingency does not crystallize into a large cash outflow.

book_subsections.title: The Arbitration Footnote and Dividend Discipline
paragraphs: No forensic balance-sheet review of EIL is complete without reading Note 4 of the Q2 FY27 financial statements, which discloses a ₹409.61 crore (₹40,960.75 lakh) legal claim pending before the Hon'ble Supreme Court. While management contests the claim, an adverse ruling would equal nearly 59 percent of FY26 net profit, or roughly a quarter of the company's ₹1,707 crore investment portfolio. Investors who ignore contingent liabilities in PSU contractors often learn about them the hard way.

On the positive side, EIL has maintained a remarkably shareholder-friendly dividend payout ratio of 38 to 49 percent over the past five years, including a ₹1.50 per share interim dividend declared alongside Q2 FY27 results. Because the core Consultancy business consumes very little maintenance capex, EIL can return nearly 40 percent of profits to shareholders while still keeping its balance sheet virtually debt-free.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Debt-Free Beats Aggressive Bidding
book_callouts.text: In engineering and EPC, leverage and fixed-price turnkey risk are a lethal combination, as Petrofac proved. EIL's ₹16 crore debt load and 75% consultancy backlog ensure it can walk away from toxic contracts rather than bid for cash flow.
